title: The ULTIMATE Back/Lats Exercises Tier-List (Yujiro-tier to Peewee-tier)
summary: NH ranks 34 lat and mid-back exercises from Peewee tier (worst) to Yujiro tier (best). His core rule is that the stretch builds the lats: pull-ups, sternum pull-ups, pullovers, dumbbell rows, close neutral-grip pulldowns, EZ-bar incline rows, iliac pulldowns and body rows make the top tier. Deadlifts, barbell rows, cheat rows and anything that removes the stretch or brings the legs in rank low.
claims: Back training should be split into lats/mid-back, traps/upper back and lower back/posterior chain, because an exercise can be great for the lats and poor for the traps
The upper back is the slowest muscle group to develop but has the most growth potential, and a developed upper back marks a mature lifter
The deadlift is only mediocre for the lats: the lat just isometrically holds the bar close, so it builds a thick 'fridge back' with no V-taper
The Jefferson deadlift is also mediocre for lats; staggering the stance and loading one lat more is still not enough lat work
Pull-ups of every grip are top tier for lats; the best backs he has seen belong to people who do pull-ups, such as calisthenics athletes
Pull-ups made one of the biggest differences in his own back aesthetics

Grip flavours: chin-ups bias the lower lat and work the core; pronated pull-ups add more upper and mid back; neutral grip allows the best stretch with tucked elbows; wide grip is the best lower-lat builder among pull-ups
The real limit on pull-ups is tendon overuse (biceps tendon and elbow pain); rotating between grip variations makes the pain go away

The wide pronated lat pulldown is only decent: sitting on a seat removes the full bodyweight hang and stretch of a pull-up, and most machines make you pull in front instead of straight down; use it as a complement or until you can do pull-ups

A wide supinated pulldown beats the pronated version for lats because it is easier to pull low to the sternum with the elbows tucked; a pronated grip flares the elbows and shifts work to the upper back
The close-grip neutral lat pulldown is top tier: elbows tuck easily, full overhead stretch, comfortable on the shoulders, and the close grip lets you stay tight and move more weight with better form
Pronated ring rows are only decent because the grip biases the upper back; supinated ring rows are excellent for the lats
On supinated rows, chin-ups and pulldowns the biceps is only an accessory mover; if it becomes the main mover you are doing the movement wrong
Bodyweight ring rows tend to fail for reasons outside the back, such as grip giving out in heavier lifters; on a neutral pulldown the grip is a non-factor
Calisthenics are king for upper back development, but adding free weights gets you further
The dumbbell row is top tier and underrated just because it is old news; you can build a monster back with it
Do dumbbell rows tripod style in a staggered stance rather than with a knee on the bench; it is healthier long term and lets you rotate the hips without straining the abdomen and risking a hernia
On dumbbell rows let the lat stretch and catch the weight at the bottom, even rotating inward; the bottom is where most of the muscle is built and the top squeeze is just a bonus

The Kroc row is slightly inferior to the dumbbell row: it is grip-heavy, invites explosive reps without negative control, and the more open elbow recruits more upper back; he uses it slowly as a rotation and likes its pendulum swing at the bottom
The renegade row is Peewee tier: the floor removes the stretch, so you only get the squeeze, and balance and core limit the load instead of the back
The straight-arm pulldown is only decent: the cable takes away the loaded stretch and its real benefit is the squeeze, so use it as a pump finisher at the end of a workout
Pullovers are top tier: unmatched lat stretch and rib cage expansion. They transformed his physique and gave him lat flare he never had, visible even relaxed
The weak point of pullovers is that the shoulders and rotator cuff link the rib cage to the weight, so use proper form and higher rep ranges; dumbbells suit most people
'Expanding the rib cage' does not mean it inflates like a balloon; it means the lats shape it and fill the side between armpit and waist
The Yates row is excellent for lower lat and mid back: supinated grip, very vertical torso, row to the belly button. The supinated grip carries biceps-tear risk; Dorian Yates tore his biceps on it
He skips Yates rows because he protects his fragile biceps tendons; they are not obligatory for lower-lat development

The barbell row is only decent for lats and upper back: it is diffuse, uses the legs and posterior chain, is hard to progressively overload without cheating, and its systemic fatigue leaves less energy for direct upper back work
5x5 and StrongLifts-style programs do not give an aesthetic upper back; he would rather have spent his first year on calisthenics and pull-up bar work

The cheat barbell row is Peewee tier: it is more of a deadlift, has no controlled negative, a worse stimulus-to-fatigue ratio for the upper back than deadlifts, and a higher injury risk; he used to do them
The seal row is excellent because the legs are out of it and you know exactly what the back gets; for lats, row toward the belly button and let the bar swing out and back in a pendulum arc

The Pendlay row is mediocre for lats: torso parallel to the floor, the floor cuts the stretch and there is no controlled negative. It is better for pulling strength, traps and upper back; he still does them with a snatch grip to the sternum
Machine rows are excellent and as good as dumbbell rows; if the machine blocks your stretch, go one arm at a time with your body shifted to the side

The sternum (Gironda) pull-up is the best of the best because it mixes vertical and horizontal pulling, but you need about 10 chest-to-bar pull-ups before attempting it; he can barely manage it himself
The seated two-hand cable row is only decent: results depend heavily on the machine, and both hands at once limit the stretch
Best back tip: your arms are just hooks; the back initiates the pull and the elbow should not drive it, and you should not rock the torso back and forth
The one-arm seated cable row is excellent and better than the two-arm version: you can wrap around for a full lat stretch and re-tuck for a better contraction without hitting yourself
The kipping pull-up is Peewee tier: no controlled negative, momentum instead of a stretched lat, and he claims it is the top cause of rotator cuff injuries in CrossFit
Pull-up tendinitis comes from dropping too deep into a dead hang and disengaging the scapula, which puts the load on tendons; keep the upper back engaged and the negative slow
The T-bar row is a noob trap he would ban: people always cheat with the knees and torso, and the two-hand handle blocks the squeeze and the inward arm rotation that involves the lats

The Meadows row is excellent: single arm, easy to find your angle and follow the arc that benefits the lats; it falls short of top tier because the staggered stance still loads the lower back, glutes and hamstrings
The Nautilus pullover machine is top tier and the holy grail of old-school lat machines; replicas still work
On the Nautilus pullover the supinated grip at the top can overextend and tear the biceps
The standing cable pulldown is Peewee tier: it becomes a momentum-driven unbalanced row; sit down and do a real pulldown
Plate-loaded chest-supported row machines are mediocre: they are rarely adjustable, so you cannot row to the belly button, and the pad crushes the sternum, which makes heavy stretched sets miserable
The rowing machine is Peewee tier for the back; it is a full-body cardio exercise driven by the legs
Cable pullovers give a tremendous stretch but are a nightmare to set up, so prefer dumbbell pullovers if you can do them
The EZ-bar incline chest-supported row is top tier and better than the seal row: the bench height guarantees a full bottom stretch and the EZ bar allows a comfortable closer grip
Dead hangs are Peewee tier for lats because the lats are disengaged; people who did weighted hangs reported zero lat growth. They are good for forearms and spinal decompression
The front lever is mediocre for hypertrophy: huge technical demand for little lat stimulus; calisthenics athletes built their lats with pull-ups, not levers
A muscle looking contracted during an exercise does not mean it is working hard
Chest-supported dumbbell rows on an incline bench are excellent, just as good as a seal row if your gym lacks one
The one-arm pull-up is mediocre: nobody controls the negative, so there is no stretch; it is a show-off skill built by people who already have strong backs
The diagonal (iliac) pulldown is top tier, but only if you go heavy for 8-10 hard reps to failure with progressive overload, not baby weights for 15 reps
The TRX inverted row is Peewee tier: too vertical and too much arm
Behind-the-neck pulldowns and pull-ups are only decent: easy to impinge the shoulder, you end up pulling in front, and they hit the upper back and rhomboids more than the lats

The body row between parallel dip bars is top tier and underrated: big stretch, tucked elbows, a pendulum motion, neutral grip that forces lat stretch, and it is easy to load with plates or a backpack
Do body rows for sets of 20-25 at the end of a workout or at a park on days you skip the gym
The muscle-up is only decent for back hypertrophy because it is half a pull-up and too technical
The towel row is Peewee tier, a resistance-free gimmick popularized by Mike Chang
The standing one-arm cable 'shotgun' row is only decent because standing encourages cheating; do it seated for hypertrophy
Kettlebell swings do not build lats; they are a posterior chain exercise, and anyone claiming big back gains from them got them elsewhere or from drugs

You do not need every top-tier lift, but a back program with none of them leaves gains on the table; S and A tier exercises are enough for a massive back, and everything below decent is laughably weak
